extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of theatre history, dramatic critics, and practising actors interested in 19th-century theatrical standards
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the criteria and standards for assessing stage acting, professional conduct, and theatrical criticism as presented in a 19th-century biographical/critical account of Edwin Forrest and the Macready controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repose as the final grace of art
rubrics_metrics.description: "Repose is the final grace of art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting should achieve repose — calm, stately, measured delivery — so that powerful moments spring forth "without effort." Example: Athenæum praised Forrest's Macbeth as "calm and stately, almost a sculpturesque, piece of acting." Contrast: earlier extravagance and constant effort are faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force should be moral, not merely physical
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting force ought to be more than physical display; it should be of a 'moral' kind rooted in inner truth rather than mere physical vehemence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism described earlier Forrest as having "force... more of a physical than a moral kind," akin to melodrama. Improvement consists in channeling raw power into studied emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free enthusiasm and sincerity vs rigid mannerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'free enthusiasm, the breathing sincerity and impassioned power' over 'cold and measured style... rigid mannerism and studied artificiality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The national contrast (American free feeling vs English measured manner) is used to evaluate qualities: sincerity and spontaneous feeling are praised; affected, mannered artifice is faulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and dignified deportment
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor's presence should be commanding and deportment dignified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics assess if 'presence is commanding' and 'deportment dignified' (negative example: review saying 'His presence is not commanding, nor his deportment dignified').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained imaginative feeling of nobleness
rubrics_metrics.description: An assumed grandeur must be supported by an imaginative sense of nobleness; gestures or airs of grandeur must be justified by inner conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative example: 'the assumption of grandeur is not sustained by an imaginative feeling of nobleness.' The criterion tests whether external manner arises from an internal conception of the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion must be truthful and sustained, not forced
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion in performance should appear as authentic feeling, not as a violent effort or mere physical exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics faulted performances described as 'a violent effort of physical vehemence.' Good practice: build passion so it comes naturally and is varied, not a series of shouts or brute displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenderness must not be affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of tenderness should be genuine rather than affected or artificial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative example from a hostile review: 'Even his tenderness is affected.' Actors should avoid mannered sweetness that reads as imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid melodrama in tragic roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic roles require depth and truth; acting 'more akin to melodrama than to tragedy' is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melodramatic behaviors (overblown gestures, crude effects) undermine tragedy. The standard is a measured, psychologically grounded delivery rather than pantomimic excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible and sustained physical characterization of age
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical signs (palsied head, tottering walk, feeble footsteps) used to portray age must be consistently maintained and credible throughout the performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Times praises Forrest's consistent assumption of old age in Lear. Fault is when physical detail is inconsistent or merely cosmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful study of the author's meaning; avoid petty point-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation should show careful, attentive study of the playwright's meaning, steering clear of fine-drawn subtleties and tricky point-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Times: Forrest 'gave evidence of the most careful and attentive study of the author's meaning, steering clear... of tricky point-making.' The ideal combines fidelity to the text with clarity of conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuance in scenes of madness and emotional variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mad scenes and complex emotional states should be shaded with nicety so features express alternation of light and darkness in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise: mad scenes 'shaded with admirable nicety,' showing minute study and varied expression rather than uniform hysteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical power should be appropriate and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Displays of physical power should be justified by the role and moment; gratuitous physical display is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Times notes that while physical power can be effective, it must be 'called for and necessary.' Avoid showy strength for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not monopolize the stage or belittle co-actors
rubrics_metrics.description: A good actor does not seek to monopolize everything or add lustre to his part by belittling others' parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forrest praised for not striving to monopolize or 'add greatness and lustre to his own part by belittling and darkening the parts of others.' Cooperative ensemble ethics are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applaud and acknowledge merit in others
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional conduct includes readiness to applaud merit in fellow actors and rejoice in their praise when deserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive professional ethic: being generous in praise rather than engaging in underhanded rivalries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid underhanded practices: bribery, anonymous manipulation, and slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity-driven tactics (persuading critics, writing anonymous pieces, bribery, slander) are condemned as dishonest professional behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Garrick, Voltaire) show the practice of manipulating public opinion via anonymous writings. The standard condemns such manipulations as moral faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pride from vanity in professional ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride (resenting unfair attacks but not attacking others) differs morally from vanity (monopolizing praise and using underhanded means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts pride (e.g., Webster, Forrest) with vanity (e.g., Garrick): pride demands a fair field and may fiercely repel affronts, but does not buy favor or slander rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of biased criticism due to cliques and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Press judgments can be biased by social cliques, patronage, and managerial influence; critics may be recipients of 'constant attentions' from a favored clique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account warns readers that reviewers may be influenced by friendships, aristocratic patrons, or managerial tactics, so newspaper praise or blame can reflect social alliances rather than pure merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware organized audience manipulation (claques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience reactions may be manufactured by 'claqueurs' or organized bodies placed to hiss or applaud, thereby distorting genuine public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the account describes three solid bodies of claqueurs who produced hisses to overpower legitimate approval. Such manipulation undermines the authenticity of reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: National bias affects theatrical reputations
rubrics_metrics.description: National feeling colors critical appraisals: local audiences and critics may favor native actors over foreigners and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative shows English critics and society aligning with Macready while the general populace favored Forrest; reviewers' national sympathies shape their judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial tactics can be unethical influences on actors' careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers may use casts or other devices to vex actors or attempt to break engagements for pecuniary reasons, which is an unethical professional tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a manager 'purposely vexed' Macready by casts to make him break engagement; such practices distort fair artistic evaluation and employment.
